Bealiah
bee-a-LIE-ah
n. (proper name; a Benjamite who came to David at Ziklag)
Hebrew Be'alyah, the LORD is lord or Jah is master, from ba'al (lord, master) with the divine element -yah — a name that takes the word used of the Canaanite god and claims it for the LORD.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Bealiah is named once: “Eluzai, and Jerimoth, and Bealiah, and Shemariah, and Shephatiah the Haruphite” (1 Chronicles 12:5). He was one of the Benjamites, Saul's kinsmen, who joined David in his outlaw years. His name repays attention more than most. Ba'al was the ordinary Hebrew word for a lord, an owner, a husband — and it was also the name of the Canaanite god. Bealiah's parents took that word and bolted it to the covenant name: the LORD is lord. The compound is a polemic. It refuses to surrender a good word to an idol, and insists that whatever mastery Baal claims belongs in fact to Jehovah. Later, when the name had become too compromised to use, Hosea records that God would remove it from Israel's mouth altogether (Hosea 2:17). But in David's day a man could still be named the LORD is lord and mean it as a challenge. The dictionary commends the instinct: the answer to a word captured by error is often to take it back, and the deeper answer is always to confess who is in fact Lord.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Bealiah is a Hebrew proper name and has no entry in Webster's dictionary of the English language.

expand to see more

Bealiah is a Hebrew proper name; Webster's 1828 dictionary treats common English words and does not define it.

The name appears once, in 1 Chronicles 12:5.

He was a Benjamite who came to David at Ziklag.

The name joins ba'al (lord) with the divine element -yah.

The sense is the LORD is lord, or Jah is master.

Key Scripture

1Ch 12:5 — "Eluzai, and Jerimoth, and Bealiah, and Shemariah, and Shephatiah the Haruphite,"

Hos 2:17 — "For I will take away the names of Baalim out of her mouth, and they shall no more be remembered by their name."

1Ki 18:21 — "And Elijah came unto all the people, and said, How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him. And the people answered him not a word."

Psa 24:1 — "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein."

Modern Corruption

Words captured by error are often surrendered; Bealiah's name takes 'lord' back and gives it to the LORD.

expand to see more

When a good word is seized and corrupted, the common instinct is to abandon it, and much ground has been given away that need not have been. The name Bealiah shows the other course: ba'al meant lord, an idol had taken the word, and a Hebrew father fastened it to the covenant name as a confession. Hosea shows the limit of the strategy, for a word can become so soaked in a false meaning that God Himself removes it.

The principle to recover is that lordship is not a contested question but a settled one. “The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof” (Psalm 24:1). Elijah's challenge on Carmel put it as a choice because the people were behaving as though it were one; the fact was never in doubt. Whether a word is reclaimed or relinquished, the confession must be made.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Be'alyah, the LORD is lord; a Benjamite of David's company at Ziklag.

expand to see more

Hebrew Be'alyah, from ba'al (lord, master) with the element -yah.

Ba'al is the ordinary Hebrew word for a lord, owner or husband.

It is also the name of the chief Canaanite god.

The compound confesses that the LORD, not Baal, is master.

The single occurrence is 1 Chronicles 12:5.
